newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma launches tourism year, ignoring criticism.
newsitem.headline: Burma launches tourism year, ignoring criticism.

text.p: Burma's military government, ignoring foreign criticism and calls for boycotts, launched its official tourism year on Monday with ceremonies featuring dancing, music and traditional costumes.

The inauguration of Visit Myanmar Year -- the government's strongest effort ever to open the once-isolated country to foreigners -- looked more like an Olympic opening ceremony than the launch of a tourism year.

Parachutists, dancing elephants and floats were part of the three-hour long ceremony in a Rangoon stadium. The military showed its presence by barking out orders to rows of colourfully dressed performers.
Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt, head of military intelligence and Secretary One of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), officially opened the tourism year.

"Today is a red-letter day for tourism in Myanmar (Burma). We are celebrating not only the launching of Visit Myanmar Year...but also our commitment to open our doors to the world," he told thousands of Burmese, diplomats and foreign businessmen who packed into the stadium.
He said the SLORC had achieved peace and stability in Burma and tourists could travel across the country without worries.
Burma has only had a tourism ministry for four years and previously had strict limits on where tourists could travel. It hopes to lure up to 300,000 tourists over the next 12 months.

But the launch of "Visit Myanmar Year", which uses the SLORC's name for Burma, comes as the military rulers face renewed criticism for their latest crackdown and continued suppression of the democracy movement led by Aung San Suu Kyi.
Since May, the government has arrested and released nearly 1,000 pro-democracy supporters for trying to attend various meetings of Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party.
Ten days ago, the motorcade in which Suu Kyi and other supporters were travelling was attacked by hundreds of stone-throwing, stick-wielding men.
Suu Kyi, the 1991 Nobel Peace laureate, blamed the government for orchestrating the incident.
Western governments and human rights groups condemned the attack and the SLORC's continued refusal to hold talks with the NLD on how to bring democracy back to Burma.
The government denied involvement in the attack and said it was just another move by the democracy movement to dissuade tourists from visiting the country.

Since her release from six years of house arrest in July 1995, Suu Kyi has urged foreign tourists to boycott Burma, saying the tourism push only benefits a handful of people -- mainly connected to the government.

Human rights organisations say the SLORC forcibly displaced people to build hotels or improve infrastructure as part of the preparations for Visit Myanmar Year. They also said the government used forced labour for infrastructure projects.
Khin Nyunt recently said Visit Myanmar Year will help negate recent bad reports about Burma.
"The main purpose of Visit Myanmar Year 1996 is to enable many tourists to visit Myanmar and see the facts," he said.
"On their return, they will explain the true situation they experienced and all the fabrications will be rebutted."
